cases.question: A complex number z has modulus 10 and a complex number omega has modulus 1. What is the maximum possible value of tan^2(theta), where theta is the argument of (omega - z)/z?
cases.source_question: Let \( \omega \) and \( z \) be complex numbers such that \( |\omega| = 1 \) and \( |z| = 10 \). Define \( \theta = \arg\left(\frac{\omega - z}{z}\right) \). Determine the maximum possible value of \( \tan^2 \theta \).
cases.independent_analytic_certificate: Let u=X+iY=(omega-z)/z, so (X+1)^2+Y^2=1/100. With s=Y/X, real solutions require discriminant4-4(1+s^2)*99/100>=0, giving s^2<=1/99. Equality at X=-99/100,Y=sqrt(99)/100 is attainable with z=10 and omega=10(u+1), which has modulus1. Thus the exact maximum is1/99.

cases.question: Let V be a vector space with an ordered basis B = (v1, ..., vn). Let T be an invertible linear operator on V such that T(v1) = 1(v1 + ... + vn). Let A be the matrix of T with respect to B. What is the sum of all entries of A^{-1} with respect to B?
cases.source_question: Let $B = \{ v_i \}_{i=1}^n$ be a basis of a vector space $V$, and let $T: V \rightarrow V$ be a linear operator such that $T(v_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i$. Find the sum of the elements of the matrix $[T^{-1}]_B$, where $[T^{-1}]_B$ is the matrix representation of the inverse of $T$ with respect to the basis $B$. Provide your answer as a single number.
cases.independent_analytic_certificate: For the reconstructed premise c=1, Ae1=ones. Invertibility gives A^-1 ones=e1. The sum of every matrix entry is ones^T A^-1 ones=ones^T e1=1. This uses no assumption about the other columns beyond invertibility.

cases.question: What is the limit as $n$ tends to infinity of $\dfrac{x_n}{n}$, where $x_n$ is the $(n)$-th root of 1 plus the sum from $k=2$ to $n$ of $(k-1)(k-1)!$?
cases.source_question: Compute the limit \( \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty }\frac{x_{n}}{n} \) for the sequence \((x_{n})_{n\geq 2}\) defined by \(x_{n}=\sqrt[n]{1+\sum_{k=2}^{n}(k-1)(k-1)!}\).
cases.independent_analytic_certificate: The telescoping identity (k-1)(k-1)!=k!-(k-1)! gives x_n=(n!)^(1/n). Stirling yields log(n!)=n log n-n+O(log n); dividing by n and subtracting log n gives log(x_n/n)=-1+o(1), hence limit1/e. The high clue gives general alpha asymptotics, whose logarithmic divergence vanishes only at alpha1. The student inserts alpha1 into the question.
